a_text: {target} with one trial has the same two possible outcomes and success probability $p$. This is the single-trial building block of a binomial count.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: {target} is the special case $n=1$. A binomial count with $n$ trials is a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli outcomes.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: {target} is the limit of a binomial count when $n$ grows, $p$ shrinks, and $np$ tends to the Poisson mean $\lambda$. The approximation is useful for rare events.{{cite:feller1968}}
b_text: {target} converges to this law when $n\to\infty$ and $p=\lambda/n$. This rare-event limit explains the Poisson count model.{{cite:feller1968}}

a_text: {target} approximates a binomial count after centring and scaling when both $np$ and $n(1-p)$ are large. The approximation keeps the binomial mean and variance.{{cite:feller1968}}
b_text: {target} is approximately normal for sufficiently large $np$ and $n(1-p)$, with mean $np$ and variance $np(1-p)$. The discrete count needs a continuity correction for tail probabilities.{{cite:feller1968}}

a_text: {target} on $(0,1)$ is exactly $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$: setting both beta shapes to one leaves a constant density.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: {target} with $\alpha=\beta=1$ is this law on $(0,1)$. Its beta density then equals one throughout the unit interval.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: {target} with two categories reduces to a beta law: its first component has distribution $\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ and the second is one minus the first.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}}
b_text: {target} is the two-category case of this law. The first probability component has beta parameters $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}}

a_text: {target} with one degree of freedom has the standard Cauchy density. A location-scale transformation gives a general Cauchy law.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: {target} with $\nu=1$ is the standard Cauchy distribution. Its missing mean illustrates why Student t moments require conditions on $\nu$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: {target} with shape $\nu/2$ and rate $1/2$ is a chi-squared law with $\nu$ degrees of freedom.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: {target} with $\nu$ degrees of freedom is this law with shape $\alpha=\nu/2$ and rate $\lambda=1/2$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: {target} is the ratio $(U/d_1)/(V/d_2)$ when independent $U$ and $V$ have chi-squared laws with $d_1$ and $d_2$ degrees of freedom.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: {target} supplies the numerator and denominator of an F ratio: independent $U\sim\chi^2_{d_1}$ and $V\sim\chi^2_{d_2}$ give $(U/d_1)/(V/d_2)$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: {target} in one dimension, with scale matrix equal to one, is a chi-squared law with $\nu$ degrees of freedom.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: {target} is the one-dimensional case of this matrix law when the scale is one. The Wishart construction generalises a sum of squared normals.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: {target} is the special case $\nu=1$: the normalising constant becomes $e^\lambda$ and the masses become Poisson masses.{{cite:shmueli2005}}
b_text: {target} extends this law by raising the factorial term to a power $\nu$. At $\nu=1$ the usual Poisson law is recovered.{{cite:shmueli2005}}

a_text: {target} counts categories whose probability vector can be given a Dirichlet prior. Updating with counts adds each observed count to the corresponding concentration parameter.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}}
b_text: {target} is conjugate for the vector of category probabilities in this sampling model. A Dirichlet prior and multinomial counts produce a Dirichlet posterior.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}}

a_text: {target} with shape one and rate $\lambda$ is an exponential waiting time of rate $\lambda$.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: {target} is the special case $\alpha=1$ of this shape-rate family. Its density then has a constant hazard.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: A {target} law with shape one is exponential with rate equal to the reciprocal of its scale. Only this Weibull shape has constant hazard.{{cite:ross2019}}
b_text: {target} with rate $1/\lambda$ is the $k=1$ case of this shape-scale Weibull law.{{cite:ross2019}}

a_text: If $X$ has {target} minimum $x_m$ and tail parameter $\alpha$, then $\log(X/x_m)$ has exponential rate $\alpha$.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: If $Y$ has {target} rate $\alpha$, then $x_m e^Y$ has this Pareto law with minimum $x_m$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: If $X$ has this F law, then $d_1X/(d_1X+d_2)$ has {target} parameters $d_1/2$ and $d_2/2$.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: If $U$ has this beta law with shapes $d_1/2,d_2/2$, then $(d_2/d_1)U/(1-U)$ has {target} degrees $d_1,d_2$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: The reciprocal of a {target} variable with shape $\alpha$ and scale $\beta$ has this gamma law with shape $\alpha$ and rate $\beta$.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: If $X$ has {target} shape $\alpha$ and rate $\lambda$, then $1/X$ has this inverse gamma law with shape $\alpha$ and scale $\lambda$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: Raising a {target} variable divided by its scale to the power of its shape gives this gamma law with shape one and rate one.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: If $Y$ has {target} shape one and rate one, then $\lambda Y^{1/k}$ has this Weibull law with shape $k$ and scale $\lambda$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: {target} counts failures before a specified number of successes in one common parameterisation. With one required success and mean failures $(1-p)/p$, that count equals a geometric trial count minus one.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: {target} counts trials through the first success; subtracting one gives this law with dispersion $\nu=1$ and mean $\mu=(1-p)/p$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: {target} approximates this without-replacement count as population size $N$ grows while marked fraction $r/N$ tends to $p$ and draw size $n$ stays fixed.{{cite:feller1968}}
b_text: {target} is the without-replacement counterpart of this independent-trial count. For fixed $n$ and a growing population with marked fraction tending to $p$, its law tends to $\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$.{{cite:feller1968}}

a_text: {target} is another positive family used in regression, but its variance at a fixed shape grows as the cube of its mean rather than the square.{{cite:mccullagh_nelder1989}}
b_text: An {target} law has variance growing cubically in its mean at fixed shape; this gamma law has variance growing quadratically at fixed shape.{{cite:mccullagh_nelder1989}}

a_text: If $X$ has this law, then $\log X$ has {target} mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. The logarithm converts multiplicative spread to additive spread.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: Exponentiating a {target} variable with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ gives a lognormal variable.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: Each single category count in this model has {target} distribution $\operatorname{Bin}(n,p_k)$, although the category counts are dependent.{{cite:forbes2011}}
b_text: A category count within {target} sampling has this binomial law with success probability $p_k$. The counts across categories sum to $n$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

a_text: Each component of this vector has a {target} marginal law, and every fixed linear combination is normal.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}
b_text: {target} in one dimension is this law; each component of a multivariate normal vector has a normal marginal distribution.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}

a_text: As dispersion $\nu$ grows with mean $\mu$ fixed, this law converges to {target} with mean $\lambda=\mu$. The extra variance shrinks to zero.{{cite:venables_ripley2002}}
b_text: {target} with mean $\lambda=\mu$ is the limit of this negative-binomial parameterisation as $\nu\to\infty$.{{cite:venables_ripley2002}}

a_text:
A {target} variable with $
u$ degrees of freedom arises as $Z/\sqrt{V/
u}$ when $Z$ is standard normal and $V$ is an independent chi-squared variable with $
u$ degrees of freedom.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
b_text: This law is a standard {target} divided by the square root of an independent chi-squared variable scaled by its degrees of freedom.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}

a_text: For integer $\nu$, a sum of $\nu$ outer products of independent centred {target} vectors with covariance $\Sigma$ has this Wishart law.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}
b_text: For integer $\nu$, independent centred vectors with this law generate a {target} matrix when their outer products are summed.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}
